title: dynamic-shape-sequence-length-handling-spec
content:
Overview:

This is a design draft for how the serving runtime should handle dynamic input shapes and variable sequence lengths. Focus areas: padding policies, bucketing strategies, and kernel selection + scheduler interactions. Goal is to reduce wasted compute from padding while keeping latency SLOs predictable and avoiding excessive scheduling complexity.

Status: draft — rough trade-offs enumerated, early perf estimates included. Plan to iterate with microbenchmarks and a small canary rollout.

Motivation / problem statement:
- Production workloads exhibit wide variability in sequence lengths: short search queries (8-32 tokens), assistant chat turns (40-200 tokens), multimodal prompts (100-5k tokens).
- Naive batching that pads all requests to the max length in the batch wastes GPU FLOPs and memory (KV cache, attention state).
- Per-request scheduling to avoid padding can increase fragmentation and reduce batch size which harms throughput. The runtime must balance latency, throughput, and cost.

Goals and constraints:
- Preserve 99th-percentile latency SLOs for interactive routes (e.g., chat) while improving average token-cost by >= 20% vs current naive padding baseline.
- Keep scheduling complexity maintainable: no heavy-weight NP-hard packing algorithms in the hot path.
- Maintain compatibility with existing KV cache semantics and support KV cache reuse for streaming + prefix caching.
- Allow operator-configurable policies: prioritize latency or cost.

Non-goals:
- Building a full auto-tuning ML model to predict lengths (outside scope).
- Handling model-specific operator fusion optimizations here — we will expose hooks for model adapters / kernels to register preferred shapes.

Current behavior (baseline):
- Batches are formed on arrival with a simple time-or-count trigger (e.g., 2ms or N requests).
- All requests in batch are padded to the longest sequence length in the batch. Kernel selection is static: we call the general-purpose attention kernel with width=max_len.
- KV cache is allocated per request with capacity tuned to model max_seq_len.
- Consequence: for skewed length distributions large waste for short requests when a long request joins a batch.

Key ideas (high-level):
1) Bucketing: group requests with similar lengths before kernel dispatch (soft bins).
2) Smart padding policies: per-bucket padding, prefix-aligned padding, and left/right padding heuristics.
3) Kernel selection: maintain multiple kernel code paths optimized for different sequence-length ranges and dispatch at runtime.
4) Scheduler integration: scheduler should be aware of buckets and dispatch per-bucket kernels, with fallback to mixed-batch execution when necessary.
5) KV cache awareness: allocate/evict KV entries in per-bucket view to avoid waste, share cached prefixes across compatible buckets.

Detailed proposals:

A) Bucketing strategies (options):
- Fixed-width bins: preconfigured bins like [1-16], [17-32], [33-64], [65-128], [129-256], [257-512], [513-1024]. Simple, low-overhead. Fast lookup. Works well if length distribution is stable.
- Dynamic histogram bins: maintain runtime histogram of recent request lengths and periodically recompute bin boundaries (e.g., quantile-based). More adaptive to workload shifts.
- Online clustering (lightweight): use incremental clustering (k-means-ish) on lengths with small k (3-8). Slightly higher CPU overhead but better fit for multimodal length distributions.

Trade-offs: fixed bins are simplest and easiest to reason about; dynamic bins reduce waste during workload shifts but add complexity. Start with fixed bins, add adaptive histogram later.

B) Padding policies (per-bucket):
- Pad-to-bin-max: pad every request in a bucket to the maximum sequence length allowed by the bin. Simple and minimizes variance inside a batch.
- Pad-to-percentile (e.g., 95th): for high-volume buckets, pad to p-th percentile of recent lengths rather than bin max to reduce worst-case padding at cost of potential truncation/progressive expansion complexity.
- Prefix-shared padding: if multiple requests share a common prefix (detected with cheap hashing), avoid duplicating KV for the prefix; only pad the divergent suffix. Requires detection but reduces memory.
- No-padding microbatches: allow very small microbatches (<M requests) to be dispatched without padding where kernels support variable shapes with masked attention (costly). This is fallback for latency-sensitive requests.

C) Kernel selection & kernel inventory:
- Kernel families:
  * short-kernel: optimized small-seqlen attention path (1-64). Tiled kernels with register-friendly loops, fused softmax.
  * medium-kernel: 65-256: uses larger tiles, reduced per-token overhead.
  * long-kernel: >=257: memory-efficient attention, favoring streaming KV updates and chunked attention.
  * mixed-kernel: supports ragged batches via per-request offsets (higher overhead).

- Kernel dispatch rules: map bucket -> kernel family. If bucket spans two kernel families, either split the bucket or use the family for the higher bound. Avoid mixed-kernel unless necessary.
- Kernel metrics: collect per-kernel throughput (tokens/sec), p50/p95 latency, and memory usage. Use these metrics for offline tuning of bin boundaries.

D) Scheduler interactions:
- Scheduler should form batches per-bucket primarily. Implementation: maintain per-bin queues and triggers (time-or-count per bin).
- Cross-bin merging: when queue sizes are low and latency SLOs permit, merge multiple small adjacent bins into a mixed-kernel batch to improve throughput. Configurable knob.
- Priority handling: interactive routes (tagged) can get explicit low-latency path: allowed microbatching w/o padding or higher scheduling priority.
- Backpressure signals: when GPU memory is constrained, prefer to schedule small bins first (to reduce peak memory usage) or drain long sequences on dedicated long-kernel workers.

E) KV cache implications and design:
- Allocation strategy: per-request KV allocations sized by the bucket's max length rather than model max_seq_len. Saves memory. For private deployments, allow operator cap to override.
- Shared prefix cache: detect identical or similar prefixes (hash + length) and allow shared KV region, copy-on-write for divergent suffix tokens. Be conservative: only enable for high-hit ratios.
- Eviction policy: LRU across buckets but weighted by predicted reuse (e.g., assistant sessions get weight).
- Consistency: ensure streaming generation still sees correct KV per request. Any shared cache must preserve isolation semantics.

Microbench experiment plan (minimum):
- Synthetic workloads: zipfian length distribution, bimodal (short+long), and heavy-tail (many very long).
- Metrics: tokens/sec, token-cost (GPU FLOPs normalized), p50/p95/p99 latency, GPU memory footprint, KV memory usage.
- Baselines: current naive padding; per-request unpadded but no batching (worst throughput); proposed bucketed padding + kernel selection.
- Expected: for bimodal workloads we expect 20-40% reduction in token-cost and ~10-15% improvement in throughput at stable latency.

API / config knobs:
- runtime.config.bucketing.enabled = true|false
- runtime.config.bins = "1-16,17-32,33-64,65-128,129-256,257-1024"
- runtime.config.pad_percentile = 100|95|90
- runtime.config.enable_prefix_sharing = true|false
- route-level override: route.config.priority = latency|throughput|cost

Implementation notes / milestones:
1) Phase 1 (MVP - 6 weeks): fixed bins, per-bin queues, pad-to-bin-max, kernel dispatch mapping. No prefix-sharing. Basic metrics.
2) Phase 2 (8 weeks): adaptive histogram-based bins, pad-to-percentile, microbatch no-padding path, kernel perf tuning.
3) Phase 3 (6 weeks): prefix-shared KV cache, cross-bin merging heuristics, rollout to dedicated workers.

Rollout plan:
- Start in internal staging with A/B tests on dev traffic.
- Canary on low-traffic routes (experimental chat routes) with route.config.priority=cost.
- Monitor p99 and increase opacity thresholds if latency regresses >5% over baseline.

Open questions / TODOs (short list):
- What is the CPU overhead for dynamic histogram update at 99th percentile load? (need microbench)
- Kernel engineering: do we already have short/medium/long kernels in repo? (Arjun: list of existing kernels please)
- How to measure prefix similarity cheaply at scale? (hashing heuristics + bloom filter?)
- Should we expose a soft-degradation mode where a long request triggers dedicated long-kernel worker instead of forcing short requests to pad? (design decision)

Notes to self / rough todos:
- Add sample flame graphs for different kernels (latency vs length).
- Sync with SRE about memory overcommit behaviour on dedicated nodes.
- Add unit tests for per-bin queue ordering and cross-bin merge thresholds.

References / links:
- GH PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/812 (kernel dispatch prototype)
- Related design doc: CONFLUENCE-RT/DOCS-214
- Jira epic: JIRA-RT-437
- Slack thread: #eng-serving-runtime (see thread pinned: "dynamic-bucketing")

Appendix: example pseudo-flow (request -> schedule):
1) Request arrives, length L estimated from tokenizer.
2) Map L -> bin B (fast lookup table).
3) Append request to per-bin queue (with metadata: route, priority, prefix-hash).
4) Bin timer or count fires -> batch selected requests up to bin_max or count.
5) If batch is mixed (cross-bin merge enabled) optionally merge adjacent bins -> determine kernel.
6) Pad to chosen pad_length (bin_max or percentile) and dispatch kernel.
7) Post-dispatch: update kernel perf metrics, update histogram counters.

End of draft.

Comments welcome — especially from kernel maintainers and SRE about memory/eviction semantics.
